hints: Look carefully at the name T-helper. Do these cells kill infected cells themselves, or do they help other cells do their jobs?
Recall what T-helper cells release after recognising antigen, and which two types of lymphocyte need that signal to become fully activated.
walkthrough:
**Remember the job of T-helper cells**

Think of T-helper cells as the coordinators of the immune response. They do not kill infected cells directly.

Their main role is to recognise antigen presented by APCs and then stimulate other lymphocytes.

**Link T-helper cells to B-lymphocytes and T-killer cells**

Once activated, T-helper cells release cytokines (chemical signals).

These cytokines are needed to activate B-lymphocytes for humoral immunity and to activate T-killer cells for cell-mediated immunity.

**Apply reduced numbers**

If there are fewer T-helper cells, there is less cytokine signalling.

That means less activation of B-lymphocytes, less activation of T-killer cells, and therefore less production of plasma cells and antibodies.

options.A: T-helper cells do not destroy infected body cells. That killing job belongs to T-killer (cytotoxic T) cells.
options.B: B-lymphocytes need cytokines from T-helper cells to become activated. Fewer T-helper cells means decreased B-lymphocyte activation.
options.C: T-killer cells also need activation by T-helper cells, so their activation would decrease, not increase.
options.D: Plasma cells develop from activated B-lymphocytes, so with less B activation, plasma cell production would decrease, not increase.
